text_fidelity_a:
PANASONIC Wings Sport Headphones are Ultra-Light Wireless Bluetooth Sport Earbud 3D Flex Sport Clips with Microphone and Call/Volume Controller, IPX5 Rated Water-Resistant - RP-BTS35-K (Black) I received these earphones from Amazon Vine in early January, 2018. I liked the over-the-ears design. It makes the earphones far less likely to fall off when exercising. The sound quality is also excellent. I found its wireless bluetooth function quite handy for listening to music on my smartphone while walking, biking, lifting weights or doing calisthenics.

In short, as long as the battery could be charged, these sport earphones worked quite well. But suddenly, a few weeks ago, after only 7 months of use, the battery simply would no longer take a charge. The manual says that the battery should last through up to 300 charges, and there is absolutely no way that in only seven months I charged this device 300 times. It holds a charge well while the battery is working, much better than the other bluetooth earbuds that I have owned. So I could use it for up to five days without charging the battery. This means that, in seven months, I only charged the battery about 42-50 times, at most. This means the life of the battery was a mere 16% of what the manufacturer promised!

This is not a device in which the battery can be replaced. Therefore, once the battery dies, the earphones are worthless. Since the warranty is only for 90 days, there is no recourse with the manufacturer for replacing this device after that length of time.

The way that this product works is a good idea, but until the design includes the possibility of replacing the battery, the high price is simply not worth it. I will have to stick to cheap earbuds which are not such a hit to my pocketbook when their non-replaceable battery dies.

I rate this product as follows:

Sound quality 5 stars
Durability of battery: 1 star
Value for price: 1 star
Overall average: 2.3 stars
text_fidelity_b: PANASONIC Wings Sport Headphones are Ultra-Light Wireless Bluetooth Sport Earbud 3D Flex Sport Clips with Microphone and Call/Volume Controller, IPX5 Rated Water-Resistant - RP-BTS35-K (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Linksys N300 Wi-Fi Wireless Router (E900) As a wireless router, this works pretty much like any other, so I thought I'd use it for another purpose: wireless networking between computers in a household that does not have internet (since this is the situation for many people).
For that usage, here's the review:

Appearance: This is a very streamline wireless router with 4 hardline ports. It's small and flat, good for a desk. The problems I have with the design are that it HAS to lie flat, and you can't mount it on a wall. Depending on how cluttered your desk area is may cause some issues.
-3 out of 5 stars

Setup: This router comes with a generic setup CD which assists not so tech savvy users to setup their wireless network using minor cables and a CD. During the CD installation it has "Show Me" buttons to assist users on actions they need to take. A large problem with this router is that you can't setup the router without an active internet connection. I attempted to use the 192.168.1.1 to manually setup the router without using the CD and was met with obstruction requiring me to run their software. This would be a bad router for local home groups without an internet connection. Attempted to connect wirelessly and was granted access to setup things like the security to connect, the security options are minor and only seem to allow WPA2-Personal security with the standard AES encryption. Because this is intended more for internet than networking, this won't count much against the overall product, so
-3 out of 5

Usability: I did the connection with my laptop and walked around to see if the signal would drop. I made it out to the street corner from where the router was placed, this was about 200ft. I still received a single bar signal out at the corner. A recommendation for the router if you are using it to broadcast an internet signal that it is password protected using both letters UPPERCASE and lowercase with numbers and symbols. This will help protect your network and any data stored on your computers. Even though the range on this router was pretty good the minor security options make it difficult to give it above a 3 out of 5.
-3 out of 5

Reliability: I attempted to reset the router back to factory by resetting it and letting it sit for about 15minutes. The router kept all information including the Name and the Password. This is both good and bad if there is a short power outage you don't have to worry about resetting passwords and the router information however if you ever lose your password you might not be able to restore it back to factory.
-3 out of 5
text_fidelity_b: Linksys N300 Wi-Fi Wireless Router (E900)

Computer Speakers, PC Speakers with 6 Colorful LED Modes, USB Powered Computer Speakers for Desktop with 2 Bass-Boost Ports, 2 Speaker Units and 3.5mm Aux-in Cable for PC, Laptop, Tablet, Phone [[VIDEOID:e1ecfa5e6b7fdff679f691ee32a8937f]] I have a very nice laptop with Bang and Olufsen built-in speakers. But, they could never sound as good as a nice set of external speakers.

I watch a lot of videos and listen to music through my laptop and was always left wanting for better sound. I ordered this set of Nylavee speakers based on a recommendation from a 'gamer' friend.

Being a gamer, a lot of his experience is based on the light show. I got to watch and listen as he went through some multi-player war games and was really impressed with the quality of the sound coming from his speakers. I'm not a gamer. The light show wasn't that important to me. However, the color changing LEDs are pretty cool. So, I bought this set for myself.

Here at home, I'm still impressed at the sound. The treble is nice a crisp. The bass is good enough that I don't think I would need a subwoofer set. The lights are easily controlled through the touch switch at the top of the right-hand speaker.

I have only one nit to pick at. The speaker's faces should be mirror images of each other, not duplicate. The way they are now, it looks like two left speakers, instead of a left and right. This is minor. But, still bugs me.

Otherwise, this is a really good set of computer speakers for the money and I am very comfortable with giving these Nylavee speakers five stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Basics Adjustable Tablet/iPad Mount Holder for Microphone and Music Stand, Black So when I ordered this mount, it was based on the title description and one small photo. Here's what I've learned since.

It's meant to be mounted to a post like what might be a part of a monitor stand. So the clamp is the shape of a hook. It does not clamp well onto flat surfaces. I wanted to mount this onto a shelf board, so I've got a plastic tube inserted on the hook side to occupy space to help it sit flat.

The holders are not spring loaded. Each end is tighten by a knob. The knobs can be difficult to access depending on the orientation of the arm. In my case one of the knob was right up against the arm. So you don't just walk up and slide you tablet into this, it needs to be set up.

The rounded retainers are plastic, not rubber. So you can't just have them on both sides. The have to be on the top or bottom or in opposing corners.

As a tablet it holder, it works. But there are far more user friendly designs out there.

I hope you found this review a little bit helpful. Thank you for reading.

Using the app Battery HD to measure charge time and level, the new charger saved about 15 minutes to go from a 15% charge to a 100% charge versus the original charger. Faster, but not a huge gain. I expect that the differential in terms of charge time for the new Fire (especially the 8.9 inch one) will be much greater when comparing this charger with using a USB port to charge. I'll post results once I have my 8.9 inch Fire.

While it's not a compelling purchase if you have the original Fire, it is worth getting (at 50% off) if ordered with a new HD Fire, especially if you can also get the MP3 credit. I'm giving it 5-stars since, at the price paid, it's very handy to have as a spare charger, and it's MUCH easier to take along than the original Fire charger.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Kindle 9W PowerFast Adapter for Accelerated Charging

At this price, it's not unexpected, but I'm having trouble figuring out an optimal use for it.

The version of Windows (S mode) it uses, won't install most software. You can only install from the Windows store. The best use I can think of for this is that my dad is too old to learn new tricks and could really use a new laptop that functions better than his ancient one, and can't install malware.

The problem is, people who aren't good with computers generally just want to buy a cheap one because they figure they won't use it much. It's self fulfilling. They aren't generally a pleasure to use. In this case, it doesn't have a touchscreen. These days, anyone who isn't between the age of 30 and 50 is probably pushing on their screen when you tell them to click something.

It includes a full tenkey on the keyboard. I would usually like that. Maybe they just had extra space and figured why not? I can't think of who would need the feature. Everyone I can think of who would want a tenkey would be dealing with either gaming or spreadsheets, and would have a nicer machine. At this point I'm thinking maybe a business that wants to cheaply equip a bunch of employees with something they can't screw with in a way that will be problematic. I think it would work fine for that, so long as there is no non-app software that needs to be installed.

Sabrent 4 Port Portable USB 3.0 Hub for Ultra Book, MacBook Air, Windows 8 Tablet PC - Black (HB-RU34) This is a great choice if you need a USB hub but don’t have much room. It’s only 1.25 inches wide and 4.75 inches long. Very slim profile that makes it easy to fit onto a desk or next to a laptop.

The 4 USB 3.0 output ports are arranged along the top; the input port is on the end. As shipped, this is a passive port (e.g., no external power) but it does have a power input at the end for a DC 5V input. The power transformer needed is NOT included in the package. The only attachment included is a USB input cord.

There is an indicator LED to show it is receiving power. I didn’t have any problems using it with USB 3.0 and 2.0 devices. However, since it’s a passive hub, it’s not the best choice for really power-hungry devices, such as large external drives or for tasks such as charging a tablet. Those applications are better suited to a hub with an external power source.

The build quality seems very good. It’s plastic, but the case feels pretty durable. The ports are well-anchored and didn’t move when I stressed the input cables.

It’s well worth considering if you need a slim profile passive hub for USB 3.0 devices.

Belkin 6-Outlet Surge Protector with 3-Foot Cord (Plus An Extra 6-Foot Extension Cord) I'm confused. I thought when I got this surge suppressor that the extension cord was meant to be used with it so you'd have a total of nine feet of cord if needed. Apparently, the extension cord doesn't actually fit the surge suppressor; the extension cord has three two-prong receptacles that you could plug, say, lamps and the like into, but you cannot plug the surge suppressor itself into it. The extension cord is clearly marked as being for two-wire polarized, as opposed to three-prong grounded, appliances. So that's more than a little misleading.

The surge suppressor looks heavy-duty, but you are cautioned in the packaging literature that it's not to be used with "sensitive equipment" like everything we use surge suppressors for: computers, TV, etc. You can't use it with things involving water, either, like aquariums. So what would I use it for? A blow dryer? I think not. To make it even worse, you are told to cover the receptacles on the extension cord if they are not in use. There are little plastic sliders that you're supposed to use for this purpose. But one of the sliders on the extension cord I received won't stay closed. China-cheap.

Belkin has some good products, but this one doesn't impress me very much. And the whole thing is packaged in one of those awful clamshells that you risk hurting yourself on when you take the scissors to it.
text_fidelity_b: Belkin 6-Outlet Surge Protector with 3-Foot Cord (Plus An Extra 6-Foot Extension Cord)

It was packaged nicely/professionally even though it is refurbished & came with charging/mounting accessories. I already have 3 Arlo cameras from before and wanted to add an additional camera and read that the Arlo Pro worked more efficiently than the Arlo 2. I struggled the first night setting it up (otherwise a very fast system to set up). I had placed it in a window which prohibited the motion device, so I ended up mounting it outside (and I do purchase the silicon skins to protect my devices) with the suggestion of Tech support and it works beautifully now (tech support wait time was less than 2 minutes on a Sunday afternoon/PST). At first, the camera appeared to have a glitch with a constant flashing, so I removed the battery and reinserted it and it was fine. Tech support was able to remote into my cameras to test whether it was getting Wifi, optimized settings, signals, etc. which was very helpful in figuring out where I was having my issue. Video is in color; it records sounds excellently; AND has a mic which I haven't accessed yet. All added features can be customized or turned off altogether (i.e., sound). In trying to set up my Pro, I watched a few Arlo videos which introduced me to the "MODE" tab option which then allowed me to access ALL my cameras in customizing my cameras better than just going straight into DEVICE tab. Not confirmed, but I think the MODE overrides any settings that you would do to your device if you go directly into DEVICE tab. Select MODE tab, then select your BASE, then click on your cameras individually & SAVE. Having accessed the MODE, ALL my cameras are now working much better. I get email alerts (which is set under MODE & can be turned off if you wish). I have had my Arlo system since 2016 and with my new addition, can't beat the price and reliability of the device. However, I do clean the lenses periodically for optimum motion detection. I do like that the Arlo Pro is rechargeable because my other 3 are not and it costs me about $40 in batteries every 3 months (those cameras take 4 batteries each).  If you find video you want to save, you can download it to your PC/Smart Phone for safe keeping; otherwise, Arlo Cloud clears your video library on the 7th day (which comes with the camera free with the option to subscribe to Arlo if you want a longer history). Bottom-line, you can purchase this system and grow it to meet your needs and upgrade cameras to which the base will support it. I can access https://arlo.netgear.com/#/login via PC or SmartPhone to view my LIBRARY. I do recommend updating your phone app periodically.

text_fidelity_a:
Canon PowerShot SX280 12.1MP Digital Camera with 20x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 3-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL) Some people have had battery problems with this camera. I bought 2 extra Vivitar batteries with higher mA-h ratings than the stock Canon batteries. If you do the math, this camera can put a huge load on the microprocessor when you ask it to take high-rate, high-resolution videos, or multiple shots. Zoom a lot at the same time, and these little batteries aren't going to hack it. In addition, Canon has something wrong (I suspect) with the battery life sensor/indicator. (My guess is the 1.0.2.0 firmware update that's available from Canon is to help that.) On the good side, that's depressed the price of this camera. Since I don't intend to take a lot of videos with this camera, I'm OK with that. :)

I may have also gotten a good one. Over 2 days of playing with it, I've yet to change the battery. It's showing 2/3 charge. It has however, flashed "charge the battery" warnings a
couple of times.

For calibration, this is replacing a Canon A1100IS we bought about 4 years ago as a second camera.

Pro (for me):
Really good, clear pictures
Good image stabilization (hand-holding at 1/15th of a second or slower!)
Low noise, as low as ISO 1600
Large zoom range
Manual focus
DIGIC 6 processor (latest generation)
Very nice screen
P, Av, Tv & M exposure modes
Canon's basically good control layout
Small and light; carrying around a DSLR can be wearying
Wi-Fi is handy
Fits in the same case as my A1100, which was originally bought for a tiny 35 mm Vivitar I carried as a 2nd camera for years. It's marked "Samsonite World Sport, Model #20" if that helps.

Cons:
Not as good a macro capability as the A1100 (which is sterling at that one thing. I'll be keeping it for that.)
No viewfinder (unlike the A1100. It's not needed all the time, but it is handy)
Slow GPS lock in (my Nexus shows 18 or so satellites in view, and took maybe 30 sec. to lock in. The camera took several times that)
GPS power hog. (It appears to suck up a lot of power, turning it on and off a few times did seem to affect battery charge indication)
No auto bracket (To be fair, that's not common on cameras, but it should be. Canon puts it on the similar S110.)
No hyperfocal distance setting (You can do it manually, of course, but, Canon, why not add another click on the focus bar? There's a computer in there, you know)
Lithium batteries (I prefer the A1100's NiMH AAs so you can get a new set at any Staples for cheap or use alkaline AAs in a pinch)

So, with all of 2 days of experience under my belt:
1) Nice easily-portable camera at a low-ish price
2) Power hog, due to inefficient GPS, big zoom, and powerful microprocessor being pushed by video, etc.
I'll update this review someday when I have some durability information.

Update: 4/27/2014 Took a nice long walk, shot 6 min. of 720p x 30fps video and took 101 L-superfine .jpg (4k x 3k pixel) photos. This used up most of a fully-charged Vivitar 1700 mA-h battery. I got a battery warn and shutdown after my walk while reviewing the video at home. The 1000 mA-h stock Canon battery would give proportionately less life. Canon says that the stock battery is good for 210 photos. A 1700 mA-h Vivitar battery should be good for 147 more than that, or 357 photos. That means that 6 min. of 720p video is worth 256 photos! I don't think anyone will be shooting at 1080p x 60fps much.

Another way to look at it is the number of pixels processed per second by any of the 11 modes of the camera. The normal L .jpg picture takes 12.0E+6 pixels/sec (12 megapixels/sec). The least hungry mode S, takes only 0.307E+6 pixels per second. The hungriest mode is the 14 frames per second L multiple shot mode, which takes 168.E+6 pixels/sec. Since this is only in use for a few frames, it's not bad on battery life. The second worst mode 1080p x 60fps takes 124.E+6 pixels per second, 1037% of the normal L photo processing power! The 720p x 30fps mode I used is only 230% of the normal L mode. Remember, though, the single shot modes are on now and then, maybe a second out of every minute at most. The video modes are on continuously.

NB: Good cameras with a lot of features have historically eaten batteries. I carry around a handful for the A1100.

Misc.: I'm sorry to see the little A1100 get superseded; it was a trouper. Its biggest problem was auto-focusing at long zoom, which isn't a problem if you're taking snapshots in your yard, but it can be a problem if you see a magnificent vista before you. The SX280 shouldn't have a problem with that (manual zoom). YMMV

Update 7/13/2014: My one significant complaint with the SX280 was the macro focusing. As I've gotten more experience with it, some of that has gone away. The SX280's autofocus seems to work differently from the A1100's. I tend to use the macro setting less, and let the normal mode carry the freight, except in extreme cases. In many cases, that's plenty good enough. It's still not as good as the A1100, though. In all other ways, this is an amazing still camera. It also still has too small a battery. Canon seems to be phasing this one out. If you need a still camera and can find one of these cheap, you might consider it.
August, 2017 Update: 3 & a bit years after purchase, the camera is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 (lens) errors more & more frequently. That's not a bad lifespan for a point & shoot, especially with a wide-range zoom lens. The error appears to be focus related.
Sept. 2018 Update: I replaced this with a 720. Much better. I actually cured the lens error with some strong blasts into the lens gaps from canned air. That's risky, blowing dust into the camera, but in this case, it worked. The 280 is now my office camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon PowerShot SX280 12.1MP Digital Camera with 20x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 3-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin 010-01689-00 Forerunner 35; Easy-to-Use GPS Running Watch, Black I did a good amount of research on other devices before buying this product. I initially wanted a sleek smartwatch that also had great fitness tracking modes, but apparently you either get a pretty smartwatch/OK fitness tracker, or a decent fitness tracker/outdated looking smartwatch. In the end I decided I wanted mainly a fitness tracker that has some smartwatch features, and that I wouldn't use most of the features on an actual smartwatch.

PROS

The app is awesome! My husband is a software developer so I learn a lot about what makes good apps good and what makes bad apps bad. This app is free and user friendly. It has mostly accurate measurements and you can easily track your progress and areas of improvement. It also has a feature that allows whoever you send the link to to track your location, in case you are concerned about getting kidnapped on your run. Very good stuff.

The steps I get seem to be pretty consistent as well as the distance traveled. The heartrate tracker seems to be mostly accurate (checked with manual pulse check).

The battery life is pretty good. Obviously I would use more battery if I am using the fitness modes. Depending on your activity level and use of the fitness modes, the battery could last you all week plus some. The battery charges to full in about 30 minutes.

I like the rectangular watch face and the light green band. I also like that you can change the bands. Apparently for some of the expensive FitBit models the band is not changeable so some people just buy a whole new watch. Like whaaat?

CONS
I like being able to see the texts I get on the watch, but I don't really care for receiving phone calls (I get so many spam calls that I don't even answer my phone lol). I don't think there is a way to say 'no' to having phone calls, so I get frequent notifications to enable phone call permissions. It's not too much of a problem but it's kind of annoying sometimes.

I think the sleep tracker is interesting, but I don't think it is accurate. I think that as long as you are "resting" during the hours that you put as your sleeping hours under Settings, that it considers this as sleep. Sometimes I can't sleep but the device considers this as light sleep. I think this would be an interesting addition, that perhaps it could be integrated: I am a night shift worker and I switch between day/night sleep, so I have to manually enter my bedtimes in the app's User Settings to sleep. I think that if there was an activity button, like when you choose walk/run/cardio on the watch itself, for sleep, it would be easier for me personally. I am not sure if that could be done with a software update or if this is a hardware type thing.

FINAL THOUGHTS

I wear this watch almost 24/7 and I think it has helped me consider and evaluate my activity levels as well as track my improvement. I think that if Garmin made a watch that had the aesthetics and watch interface comparable to the Apple watch but kept the good fitness aspect, I would definitely purchase as an upgrade.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin 010-01689-00 Forerunner 35; Easy-to-Use GPS Running Watch, Black
